subtopics: Choosing between MERGE and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Conditional Data Changes with MERGE. Its primary job is to help you change data deliberately, inspect returned rows, and keep bulk loads and destructive changes recoverable. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing conditional data changes with merge teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: change data deliberately, inspect returned rows, and keep bulk loads and destructive changes recoverable. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Conditional Data Changes with MERGE
content_blocks.expected_output: Returns ids 1 and 2, with id 1 updated and id 2 inserted. PostgreSQL 15+ supports MERGE.
content_blocks.safety_note: Only synthetic temporary data is modified.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run all statements in a disposable session. This illustrates MERGE behavior with a temporary target table.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Conditional Data Changes with MERGE”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “MERGE statement structure”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “MERGE statement structure”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Conditional Data Changes with MERGE, with an explanation of “MERGE statement structure”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Conditional Data Changes with MERGE fits into the broader goal to change data deliberately, inspect returned rows, and keep bulk loads and destructive changes recoverable.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: MERGE statement structure, Matching source and target records, Conditional inserts, updates, and deletes.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
